summary: This standards-track document extends TRILL to support multi-topology routing of unicast and multi-destination traffic, using the IS-IS multi-topology mechanism of RFC 5120. It lets a TRILL network carry traffic over separate topologies.

plainLanguage.summary: A city can have a bus map and a bike map. This lets one network keep several different maps and send each kind of traffic by the right one.

questions: how does trill support multiple topologies
what is topology zero in trill
what is the trill mt label
how does trill route multicast per topology
subtitle: How a TRILL campus can carve one physical network into several separately routed topologies.

tldr.problem: In a TRILL campus, Data packets can use any switch or link regardless of their VLAN or label, so there is no way to keep a class of traffic on, or off, certain parts of the network.
tldr.mechanism: Using IS-IS multi-topology from RFC 5120, switches advertise which topologies they support, classify each packet into a topology, and route and build distribution trees separately per topology, with an optional explicit topology label in the packet.
tldr.outcome: Operators can keep traffic on chosen switches and links, but they must configure topology classification consistently or routing loops can persist. RFC 8377 updates RFC 6325 and RFC 7177.

facts.label: Default topology
facts.value: Zero, supported by all switches and links

today: RFC 8377 is a Proposed Standard from July 2018 and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 6325 and RFC 7177.

sections.title: Why Multi-Topology for TRILL
sections.content:
This document extends TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) to support multi-topology routing for both unicast and multi-destination traffic. It builds on IS-IS multi-topology from RFC 5120. Implementation and use are optional, and use requires configuration.

Multi-topology is different from Data Labels (VLANs and Fine-Grained Labels). Data Labels describe communities of end stations, but in a single-topology campus a TRILL Data packet can use any switch and link regardless of its Data Label. In a multi-topology campus, a packet is restricted to the switches and links of its own topology.

The RFC lists example uses: separate routing domains for isolated multicast or IPv6 islands, routing a class of traffic around switches that lack some needed characteristic, or keeping a class of traffic off certain links for security or reliability reasons.

Routers must agree on how packets and links are classified. If they do not, persistent routing loops can occur, and the network manager is responsible for configuring multi-topology consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine one town with many roads, but trucks may only use some roads and bikes only others. Each kind of traveler gets its own map of allowed roads.

sections.title: Topologies, Links and Switches
sections.content:
A topology is a subset of the TRILL switches and of the links between them. Data packets are constrained to the switches and links of their topology. Topology zero is the special default base topology: all switches and links are in it and MUST support it, so it can carry management messages, BFD messages and RBridge Channel messages.

A switch advertises the topologies it supports in MT TLVs in its LSP, and in every TRILL Hello it sends on a port, except that listing topology zero is optional. There is no separate MT capability bit; advertising any topology with the MT TLV is what shows a switch is MT capable.

A link is usable for packets in a non-zero topology T only if all TRILL switch ports on the link advertise support for T, and, if any port on the link requires explicit topology labeling, every other port on the link can generate such labels.

Multi-topology applies only to TRILL Data packets. TRILL IS-IS packets and link-level control frames are link local and sit above all topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Every road is always on the everyday map (topology zero). A road only joins the bike map if everyone using it agrees it is a bike road.

sections.title: Classifying Packets and the MT Label
sections.content:
A packet's topology is commonly worked out from fields in the packet, such as payload VLAN or FGL, priority, IP version, Ethertype or DSCP bits, or from the port it arrived on. The RFC also adds an optional explicit topology label.

Support is announced in a 2-bit capability field in the Port TRILL Version sub-TLV in Hellos. Value 0 means no support. Value 1 means the port can insert labels and tolerates them, but does not need them; a packet whose label differs from the port's own classification MUST be discarded. Values 2 and 3 are treated the same: the port requires a label for every topology except zero, and treats unlabeled packets as topology zero.

The MT Label has the Ethertype 0x9A22, a version field (zero in this document), a 2-bit reserved field sent as zero, and a 12-bit MT-ID taken from the MT TLV topology number space. With it, the TRILL data labeling area has four standard forms: C-VLAN, FGL, MT C-VLAN and MT FGL. All MT switches MUST be FGL safe.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet can wear a name tag saying which map it follows. Some roads insist on the tag, some accept it, and some do not know about tags at all.

sections.title: Adjacency, Nicknames and Routing
sections.content:
Adjacency for topology zero works as before and is announced with the Extended Intermediate System Reachability TLV (#22). For a non-zero topology T, a switch reports an adjacency in the MT Reachable Intermediate Systems TLV (#222) only if the adjacency is in the Report state and the two link conditions above hold.

Nicknames are common to all topologies, just as IS-IS System IDs are. Nickname allocation uses only Nickname sub-TLVs in Router Capabilities TLVs (#242) and ignores those in MT Router Capability TLVs (#144).

Unicast packets (TRILL Header M bit = 0) use logically separate forwarding tables per topology, computed by least cost routing using only links and nodes that support that topology. The next hop is looked up by topology and egress nickname.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch keeps one name for itself that every map shares, but a separate set of directions for each map.

sections.title: Multi-Destination Traffic
sections.content:
Multi-destination packets (M bit = 1) travel over a distribution tree, so a non-zero topology T needs trees built only from links usable for T. If T is split into disjoint islands, each tree is local to one island. Only sub-TLVs inside MT Router Capabilities TLVs for T are used to pick tree roots, and tree pruning uses only the Interested VLANs and Interested Labels sub-TLVs advertised for T.

For a non-zero topology, a Number of Trees to Compute value of zero is honored and means no trees are computed. In topology zero the same value still causes one tree to be computed.

On multi-access links, a non-zero topology packet MUST NOT be forwarded onto a link that does not meet the usability requirements for that topology, even if some MT switch ports are on it. An MT switch MUST keep logically separate routing tables per topology for multi-destination traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message goes to many people, each map gets its own delivery route, and the route only visits places on that map.

sections.title: Mixed Links and Legacy Switches
sections.content:
A link can hold any mix of MT, FGL and VLAN-only switches. DRB election and Forwarder appointment work as already specified, and the network manager must configure which switch is DRB and which is the Appointed Forwarder. Frames ingressed by VL or FGL switches can only be in topology zero, and native frames cannot carry an explicit topology label.

Because older switches do not understand topologies, four sub-TLVs (Special VLANs and Flags, Enabled-VLANs, Appointed Forwarders, VLANs Appointed) MUST appear only in MT Port Capability TLVs with a zero MT-ID; occurrences with a non-zero MT-ID are ignored.

Areas of topology-ignorant switches can join an MT campus but can only ingress, transit or egress topology zero packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Older switches only know the everyday map, so they are only allowed to carry everyday traffic.

sections.title: Learning, ESADI and Channel Messages
sections.content:
Learning of end station MAC addresses is done per topology as well as per label, so the same MAC address can appear in different topologies without confusion. ESADI also runs per label per topology, with separate link state databases for each topology.

RBridge Channel messages, including BFD over TRILL, look like normal multi-destination Data packets to transit switches, so they have a topology. For network management they are generally sent in topology zero to avoid topology constraints.

On implementation size, the RFC notes that a single router handling more than eight topologies is rare in Layer 3 IS-IS MT deployments. A switch handling eight or more topologies can be considered a full implementation, and one handling four a minimal but still useful one.
sections.plainLanguage: The address book is kept separately for each map, so two houses with the same number on different maps do not get mixed up.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Multiple topologies are sometimes used to isolate or secure traffic, for example by keeping sensitive traffic off links more likely to be observed by an adversary. The RFC says delivery of data outside its topology is generally a security policy violation to avoid at all reasonable costs, and recommends IS-IS security on all IS-IS PDUs plus suitable link security, particularly between RBridges.

The IEEE Registration Authority allocated Ethertype 0x9A22 for the MT Label. IANA assigned bits 14-15 of the Port TRILL Version sub-TLV capabilities for topology labeling support and created an informational TRILL Ethertypes subregistry.
sections.plainLanguage: If a secret message is meant for one map, it must never leak onto another. Locking every road helps keep it that way.

fields.name: V
fields.desc: Version of the MT Label; this document specifies version zero.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: MT-ID
fields.desc: The topology, using the topology number space of the MT TLV.

items.label: No support
items.desc: Cannot send labels and will likely discard labeled packets; must classify by examining packets or by arrival port.

items.label: Capable and tolerant
items.desc: Can insert and tolerate labels but does not need them; discards a packet whose label disagrees with its own classification.

items.label: Label required
items.desc: Requires a label except for topology zero; unlabeled packets are topology zero. Treated the same.
